summary: Describes the input and output details for the payment application interface of the Internet Open Trading Protocol, and the procedures for using Secure Electronic Transaction as the payment protocol in version 1.0 of IOTP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When buying something online, the shop and the payment system must hand details back and forth. This memo says exactly how that handoff works for one old payment method.

subtitle: How Secure Electronic Transaction payment fits into the Internet Open Trading Protocol.

tldr.problem: The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) was designed to handle multi-party online transactions, but it needed a way to integrate SET (Secure Electronic Transaction), a payment protocol that handles credit card payments. The two protocols have different message formats and flows, so a bridge specification was needed.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3538 defines how to wrap SET payment messages inside IOTP messages, how the merchant and payment handler interact, what API calls are needed, and how to handle three types of transactions: brand-independent purchases (where the same offer works for all card types), brand-dependent purchases (where offers vary by card type), and status inquiries.
tldr.outcome: Online merchants using IOTP can now process SET payments in a standardized way, though SET itself is obsolete and IOTP is seldom deployed today.

today: RFC 3538 is an Informational document that describes a bridge between two now-obsolete protocols. SET Secure Electronic Transaction was superseded by EMV (Europay-Mastercard-Visa), and IOTP saw very limited adoption. The RFC remains a historical record of an attempt to integrate multi-party e-commerce with secure payment processing in the early 2000s.

sections.title: What IOTP and SET are
sections.content:
The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) is a framework for multi-party online transactions. It coordinates between a consumer, a merchant, a payment handler (which processes the payment) and optionally a delivery handler (which ships goods). Secure Electronic Transaction (SET) is a payment protocol specifically for credit card transactions. It includes mechanisms for merchant authentication, cardholder authentication, and fraud prevention.

This RFC describes how SET can be used as the payment method within IOTP version 1.0, specifying how SET payment messages are encapsulated inside IOTP messages and what procedures the merchant and payment handler must follow. The RFC assumes readers are familiar with both IOTP and SET specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: IOTP is a way to organize a whole transaction with many parties. SET is a way to pay with a credit card. This document explains how to use SET to pay for an IOTP transaction.

sections.title: Business rules and transaction types
sections.content:
The specification is based on SET version 1.0 and IOTP version 1.0. It covers three transaction types that are in scope: brand-independent baseline purchases (where the same offer works regardless of which card brand is used), brand-dependent baseline purchases (where the merchant adjusts prices or offers based on card type), and status inquiries (where a consumer asks about a previous payment).

The specification does NOT cover credit reversals, certificate registration, or inquiry processes. The requirements are to maintain interoperability at the payment level, not to modify SET specifically for IOTP, and to keep consistency between IOTP and SET concepts.
sections.plainLanguage: This covers three kinds of shopping trips: simple purchases, purchases where the price depends on what card you use, and asking about a past payment. Left out: refunds and other advanced things.

sections.title: How the components fit together
sections.content:
The architecture has an IOTP Application Core (OAC) that processes IOTP messages on both consumer and merchant sides. Between the OAC and the payment system is an IOTP Payment Bridge (OPB), which translates between IOTP API calls and the existing payment software (such as SET). On the consumer side, this payment bridge talks to the SET Core, which handles the actual cryptography and SET protocol. On the merchant side, it talks to a SET payment handler.

The flow is: IOTP messages travel between consumer and merchant over HTTP. When payment is needed, the OAC calls the payment bridge, which calls SET. The SET Core on the consumer side and the SET Bridge on the merchant side exchange SET protocol messages (InitReq, PInitRes, PReq, PRes) which are wrapped back into IOTP messages for transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: IOTP handles the shopping part. When it is time to pay, IOTP hands off to a payment bridge, which talks to SET. SET does the credit card work, then hands the answer back to IOTP.

sections.title: Purchase flows and API calls
sections.content:
In a brand-independent purchase, the merchant sends the offer and terms at the same time. The consumer's SET Bridge first calls FindPaymentInstrument (to find what payment methods the consumer has), CheckPaymentPossibility (to confirm the payment is feasible), and then StartPaymentConsumer (to initiate the SET handshake). The consumer's SET Core then exchanges SET InitReq and PInitRes with the Payment Handler, followed by PReq and PRes messages. The merchant simultaneously calls FindAcceptedPaymentBrand, FindAcceptedPaymentProtocol, and GetPaymentInitializationData to set up the payment bridge on its side.

In a brand-dependent purchase, the merchant first sends only a payment brand inquiry. The consumer selects a brand (e.g., Visa vs Mastercard), sends that back, and the merchant then returns the full offer including any brand-specific terms or pricing. Otherwise the flow is identical. Both finish with the consumer's bridge calling CheckPaymentReceipt and ExpandPaymentReceipt, then ChangeProcessState to mark the transaction as complete.

The RFC defines API calls organized into groups: brand compilation calls discover what payment options are available, brand selection calls let the consumer choose a method, payment transaction calls orchestrate the exchange, and inquiry calls allow checking on outcomes. Each API call specifies mandatory and optional parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to buy: merchant shows the price upfront, or asks what card first then adjusts the price. Either way, the system calls different functions to find brands, pick one, do the payment, and ask about results.

sections.title: Detailed SET protocol procedures and status inquiry
sections.content:
A status inquiry lets the consumer ask 'What happened to my payment?' The consumer's SET Bridge calls StartPaymentInquiry, which causes the SET Core to send a SetInqReq (Inquiry Request) to the Payment Handler. The handler's SET Bridge receives it, calls InquirePaymentStatus on the SET Core, and returns the result (SetInqRes) back to the consumer.

The RFC also addresses Cash Advances, where the consumer makes one payment via SET and receives a second payment by another mechanism (e.g., a check). It specifies how Process State is represented on both consumer and payment handler sides, what completion codes mean, what percentage-complete values are, and how severity levels (informational, warning, error) are used.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes wrong, the consumer can ask 'Did you get paid?' and get an answer. The document also covers getting cash instead of goods, and how to track progress.
